cues.text: A New Treason
In 1534, the Act of Supremacy declared King Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England.

An act of Parliament made it high treason to deny this claim, transforming almost overnight the plain profession of Catholic faith and loyalty to the papacy into a capital offense across England and Wales.
Where earlier medieval England had known religious dissent chiefly as a matter for ecclesiastical courts, the new treason laws transformed the ordinary practice of the historic faith.
They made it a matter of state security, punishable with the full ceremonial brutality England reserved for its most serious political crimes.
The First to Refuse
Among the earliest to die were Carthusian monks of the London Charterhouse, led by their prior John Houghton.
They refused the Oath of Supremacy on May 4, 1535, and were hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn.
This martyrdom opened, in the very same year, the executions of the far better known Thomas More and John Fisher , whose refusal for exactly the same reason has never been forgotten.

Their execution at Tyburn, carried out with deliberate public ceremony, was intended by the crown to demonstrate unmistakably that no rank of religious life, however ancient or respected, offered any shelter from the new law.
Priests Trained in Secret
As Elizabeth I's own reign hardened official policy still further, a new generation of English Catholic priests trained secretly at continental seminaries.
These seminaries were in France, Spain, and Rome, and the priests slipped back into their homeland disguised as merchants and travelers.
They celebrated Mass in secret and hid, when authorities came searching, within specially constructed priest holes concealed inside the walls and chimneys of sympathetic Catholic households.
Many of these missionary priests trained at the English College in Douai or at Rome itself.

Before setting foot again on English soil, they understood clearly that capture meant almost certain execution, and went anyway, sustained by seminaries that continued, decade after decade, to send fresh priests to replace those the state had killed.
Laypeople Among the Martyrs
The persecution reached well beyond the clergy: St. Margaret Clitherow , a York housewife who sheltered priests in her own home, was crushed to death under a weight of stones.

She refused to enter a plea that would have implicated her own children as witnesses, while others, including the printer St. Ambrose Barlow , faced execution simply for possessing or distributing Catholic literature.
Nearly a Century and a Half of Danger
Executions under these treason laws continued intermittently across five successive monarchs, from the earliest Carthusian martyrs of 1535 through the final victims of the fabricated Popish Plot .
These final victims were executed in the reign of Charles II in 1679, nearly a century and a half after 1535.
Throughout this period, the ordinary practice of the Catholic faith in England could, at any moment, cost a believer's life.

Executions were carried out publicly and deliberately, often before large crowds, as a calculated warning meant to discourage the wider Catholic population from harboring priests or attending clandestine Masses.
Legacy

Pope Paul VI canonized forty of these English and Welsh martyrs together in 1970, honoring priests and laypeople, men and women, drawn from every rank of English Catholic society, while dozens more have since been beatified individually.
Together they remain the Church's enduring witness to an England that once made the simple, quiet practice of the Catholic faith an act of treason.
Hearing Mass, sheltering a priest, or owning a Catholic book could bring the full and terrible weight of the state.
The modern nation now honors this witness, even as it once condemned it.
Their combined witness continues to remind every believer that the plainest, quietest acts of ordinary religious practice can, in the wrong political season, become the very acts that cost a life.
